Zero interest and conditional deferred interest: what a small deadline balance can change

Four charts follow purchase principal, an unposted interest memo and the deadline assessment under two explicit promotional-credit examples.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Test the payoff condition in a hypothetical promotional purchase

Interactive planning lab

Purchase principal left after the deadline top-up$240
Deferred interest posted at the deadline$338.4
Deferred plan · balance after deadline assessment$578.4

Two independently authored promotional contracts finance one purchase with identical on-time principal payments. The true-zero contract assesses no interest for the promotional months. The conditional contract records an unposted interest memo for each complete month, using that month’s OPENING purchase principal × annual quote ÷ 12, rounded to the nearest cent each month. The first payment occurs at the end of month one, not on the purchase date. Unposted memo interest does not itself earn interest. Each scheduled payment is capped at remaining principal and allocated entirely to this one purchase. After the last month-end payment, an additional selected whole percentage of the still-remaining purchase principal is received before a separate deadline assessment. If any principal remains, all memo interest is posted once; if principal is zero, the entire memo is waived. All minimum-payment and other conditions are assumed satisfied; there are no late fees, other purchases, payment-allocation conflicts, taxes or setup charges. This simplified monthly method is not a daily-interest reconstruction, APR disclosure, lender quote or universal contract rule. The endpoint is a debt balance, not a demand that the entire amount be paid immediately. No subsequent interest, repayment schedule, bank balance or source of the top-up cash is modeled.

On this page

  1. Read the condition attached to the interest promise
  2. Follow purchase principal independently of the interest memo
  3. Treat the memo as a conditional charge, not monthly cash spending
  4. Apply the payoff condition after the final principal payment
  5. Keep the promotion deadline distinct from routine billing dates

The central idea

A promotional period needs an exact payoff condition. Track the original purchase balance, actual payment dates and any interest that becomes chargeable if the condition is missed.

01

Read the condition attached to the interest promise

Two financing offers can charge no interest on the statements received during a promotion and still have different consequences at its end. A true-zero promotional contract and a conditional deferred-interest contract make different promises about those earlier months.

In this guide's true-zero example, no interest becomes chargeable for the promotional months. A remaining balance can still attract interest afterward under a real agreement, but that later period is outside this illustration.

In the conditional example, interest is recorded in a separate memo while purchase principal is being repaid. The memo is waived if the entire purchase principal is cleared by the specified deadline. Otherwise, all of that memo is posted once. The absence of a current interest charge does not establish that no conditional amount is accumulating.

FCAC explains that retail-credit consequences depend on the plan's terms. CFPB's educational discussion distinguishes zero-interest promotions from deferred-interest offers. Those sources establish the reason to inspect the condition; the schedules and monthly calculation below are original examples, rather than quoted lender terms.

02

Follow purchase principal independently of the interest memo

The default purchase is CAD 2,400. A CAD 180 payment arrives at the end of each of twelve complete months. Every payment is allocated entirely to this one purchase, with no other card balance or missed-payment condition.

Twelve payments total CAD 2,160, leaving CAD 240 of purchase principal before any additional deadline payment. That identity is the same in both hypothetical contracts: original principal minus actual principal repayments equals remaining purchase principal.

The first payment happens after the first complete month. A payment made on the purchase date would create a different balance history and therefore a different conditional-interest calculation. Payment timing belongs in the model alongside payment amount.

The principal chart stops before the optional deadline top-up. Increasing that final payment does not pretend that the same money reduced balances during earlier months. Once a scheduled payment would exceed the principal still owed, only the remaining principal is taken; the model does not create an overpayment or a negative debt.

03

Treat the memo as a conditional charge, not monthly cash spending

The example uses an annual simple quote of 24%, applied at one-twelfth per complete month. The monthly memo charge equals that month's opening purchase principal times 2%, rounded to the nearest cent. The charge is recorded before the end-of-month principal payment.

The opening principals are CAD 2,400, CAD 2,220 and so on through CAD 420 in month twelve. Their sum is CAD 16,920. At the default rate, the twelve monthly memo charges total CAD 338.40.

This is a declining-principal calculation. It does not charge twelve months of interest on the original CAD 2,400 throughout, and it does not assess twelve months of interest solely on the final CAD 240. Both shortcuts discard the intervening balance history.

The memo does not compound while unposted. It neither reduces a bank account nor increase the purchase principal being paid during the promotion. Actual contracts can use daily balances, other allocation rules or different accrual terms. The explicit monthly convention makes this exercise inspectable without claiming to reproduce those statements.

04

Apply the payoff condition after the final principal payment

After the last regular payment, the reader can add an extra payment equal to a chosen whole percentage of the remaining purchase principal. The model assumes it is received before a separate deadline assessment. At the default 0%, no extra payment arrives.

With CAD 240 still remaining, the conditional plan posts CAD 338.40 of memo interest. Its resulting balance is CAD 578.40. The true-zero example retains only CAD 240. These are amounts owed after assessment, rather than automatically assumed immediate cash withdrawals.

An extra CAD 240 clears all remaining principal before assessment. The conditional plan then waives the complete CAD 338.40 memo, leaving no balance in either example. That final CAD 240 is a repayment of principal, not an interest charge or a second purchase.

A 99% top-up pays CAD 237.60 but leaves CAD 2.40. Under the stated all-or-nothing condition, that small balance still triggers the full memo, producing CAD 340.80 owed in the conditional plan. This sharp boundary is why the comparison uses explicit scenarios rather than a smooth interpolation that suggests proportional interest forgiveness.

05

Keep the promotion deadline distinct from routine billing dates

The final month-end payment and the deadline assessment are ordered events in this model. They are not claims about a real provider's cut-off time. CFPB's explanation notes that a deferred-interest end date can differ from the regular monthly payment due date.

For a real offer, confirm the promotion's exact expiration date, how received payments are credited and the amount required to clear the relevant promotional balance. A payment instruction or pending bank transfer is not evidence that the creditor has received and allocated the money.

The illustration assumes every other condition is satisfied. It does not estimate minimum required payments, late fees, penalty rates or how payments are shared across several purchases. Those terms can affect the result before the modeled final deadline.

It also does not assign a source to the extra payment. A mathematical top-up that waives interest still needs cash available on the correct date. Connect the verified repayment amount with the household's own receipt and bill calendar before treating it as funded.

06

Use the example to ask a precise repayment question

The four charts separate purchase principal, the unposted interest memo, the final assessed balance and alternative deadline repayments. Each answers a different question. Combining them into one unlabeled running balance would make it difficult to distinguish a conditional amount from money already owed or paid.

Changing the regular payment alters the entire principal history and thus the memo. Changing only the final top-up alters the payoff condition without changing earlier accrual. If regular payments already clear all principal, every extra-payment scenario has a zero residual and the memo is waived.

A zero interest-rate input produces no memo even if principal remains. That arithmetic identity does not remove the obligation to repay principal. Likewise, a zero purchase creates no debt or interest in this fee-free illustration.

The practical comparison is the actual agreement plus a dated repayment schedule: which amount must be fully paid, which earlier-period interest can become chargeable and when payment must be received. The model stops at that assessment and makes no claim about future interest, credit approval or the affordability of the purchase.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All purchase amounts, rates and repayment terms are hypothetical. The calculator uses an explicit monthly opening-balance convention, not a reconstruction of any lender’s daily statement. It stops immediately after the deadline assessment. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
